items.explanation: ギャ is 'gya': ギ ('gi') plus a small ャ ('ya'), said as one beat. It is the same sound as hiragana ぎゃ. Combinations work the same way with dakuten and handakuten kana: ぎ, じ, び or ぴ plus a small ゃ, ゅ or ょ, said as one beat.
items.mnemonic: The big ギ swallows the little ャ: 'gi' and 'ya' squeeze into one beat, 'gya'.

items.explanation: ギュ is 'gyu': ギ ('gi') plus a small ュ ('yu'), said as one beat. It is the same sound as hiragana ぎゅ.
items.mnemonic: The big ギ swallows the little ュ: 'gi' and 'yu' squeeze into one beat, 'gyu'.

items.explanation: ギョ is 'gyo': ギ ('gi') plus a small ョ ('yo'), said as one beat. It is the same sound as hiragana ぎょ.
items.mnemonic: The big ギ swallows the little ョ: 'gi' and 'yo' squeeze into one beat, 'gyo'.
items.culture_note: Gyoza came to Japan from China, where they are called jiaozi.

items.explanation: ジャ is 'ja': ジ ('ji') plus a small ャ ('ya'), said as one beat. It is the same sound as hiragana じゃ. The i sound disappears: じ + ゃ is 'ja', not 'ji-ya'.
items.mnemonic: The big ジ swallows the little ャ: 'ji' and 'ya' squeeze into one beat, 'ja'.

items.mnemonic: The big ジ swallows the little ュ: 'ji' and 'yu' squeeze into one beat, 'ju'.
items.culture_note: ジュース is used for fruit juice but also, loosely, for sweet soft drinks in general.
